explain.tweet: Feser’s case: change, parts, abstract truths, the gap between what things are and that they are, and the demand for explanation each lead — here and now, not back in time — to something purely actual, simple and necessary. There can be only one such thing. That’s God.
explain.elevator: Feser gives five independent arguments. Each starts from something undeniable — that things change, that they have parts, that math is objectively true, that nothing in the world exists by its own nature, that things have explanations — and shows that, right now, everything depends on a cause that has no potential, no parts and no dependence at all. He then shows that anything like that must be unique, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing and good. Five roads, one destination: the God of classical theism.
explain.twoMinute:
Most people think arguments for God go like this: everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, so God — and then they ask what caused God. Edward Feser’s *Five Proofs* argues that no serious philosopher ever argued that way.

Instead, he offers five separate arguments with the same shape. Each starts with something you can’t really deny. Things **change** — your coffee cools. Things have **parts** — a chair needs its legs held together. **Mathematical truths** are objective — two plus two was four before anyone noticed. For every ordinary thing, **what it is** doesn’t include **that it is** — you can know what a lion is without knowing lions exist. And things have **explanations** — we never accept ‘it just happened’ in science.

Then each argument asks not ‘what started the universe?’ but ‘what keeps this going *right now*?’ Your coffee exists only because its molecules are actually water rather than separate gases, which depends on atoms, which depends on particles, and so on — a chain where every link has borrowed power, like a paintbrush in a painter’s hand. A chain of borrowed power can’t go on forever with no lender; however long a brush handle is, it can’t move itself. So there must be something at the bottom with nothing borrowed: something purely actual, with no parts, whose very nature is to exist.

The second stage shows such a thing must be one of a kind — there’d be nothing to tell two of them apart — unchanging, outside time, immaterial, all-powerful, and, because it’s the source of every pattern in things, an intellect that knows everything. Chapter 6 shows the five conclusions are the same being described five ways, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both naming Venus.

That’s why ‘what caused God?’ misses: the whole point is that there must be something that doesn’t need a cause because it lacks the very feature — potential, parts, borrowed existence — that makes other things need one. You can still disagree. But you have to find the false premise.
explain.eli12:
Think about a stack of books on your desk. The top book stays up because the book under it holds it. That book stays up because the next one holds it, and so on down to the desk, the floor, the ground. None of them holds itself up — each one is only borrowing its ‘holding-up power’. If everything in a stack were only borrowing, nothing would be holding anything up at all!

Feser says everything in the world is a bit like that. Your body keeps existing only because your cells hold together, which depends on molecules, which depends on atoms, and on and on — right now, this very second. So there has to be something at the bottom that isn’t borrowing anything: something that just **is**, all on its own, with no parts to fall apart and nothing that could change.

He finds this ‘bottom’ five different ways — by thinking about change, about parts, about math, about why things exist at all, and about why everything has a reason. And every way ends up at the same thing. There can only be one of it, it can’t change, it isn’t made of stuff, it’s the source of all power, and — since every idea of every possible thing comes from it — it’s a mind that knows everything. That’s what people have always meant by God.

> A good question to ask back if someone says ‘Then who made God?’: ‘Who holds up the thing that isn’t borrowing anything?’
whiteboard: Draw five boxes across the bottom labeled CHANGE, PARTS, MATH/ABSTRACT TRUTHS, ESSENCE ≠ EXISTENCE, PSR. Say: ‘Five undeniable starting points, five chapters.’

Above each box draw a vertical ladder of arrows (cup ← desk ← floor…). Label it ‘hierarchical series: here and now, borrowed power’. Next to it draw a horizontal time-line with ‘could be infinite — Feser grants it’. Stress: the ladders, not the timeline, are what matter.
At the top of each ladder write its terminus: PURE ACT; THE ONE (simple); NECESSARY INTELLECT; SUBSISTENT EXISTENCE; NECESSARY BEING. Say: ‘Stage 1 gets you here.’

Draw double-headed arrows linking the five top labels: act ⇔ simple; act ⇔ existence itself; all ⇔ necessary; necessary intellect → act. Then draw a single circle around all five: ‘There can’t be two — nothing could distinguish them.’
Inside the circle list the Stage 2 attributes: one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, omnipotent, intellect, omniscient. Say: ‘These follow from the description — no leap of faith.’
Draw a thin arrow from the circle down to every box: ‘conservation and concurrence — everything depends on it at every moment, and really acts through its power.’
Off to the side, draw a crossed-out bubble ‘Everything has a cause → universe has a cause’ and a crossed-out ‘Big Bang = first cause’. Say: ‘These are the straw men chapter 7 dismantles.’
Finish with a box labeled ‘Revelation? Miracles?’ above the circle, outside the frame: ‘Where natural theology stops and the debate among theists begins.’
explain.keyAnalogy: **The paintbrush with an infinitely long handle** (with the ‘five trails, one summit’ image for the convergence). A brush moves paint only because a hand moves it; lengthening the handle — even infinitely — adds no power of its own. That is the logic of every causal proof: a series whose members have only borrowed power needs an underived source, however long it is, and whether or not the universe had a beginning. Use it the moment someone says ‘infinite regress’ or ‘Big Bang’. Then add the summit: each of the five proofs is a different trail from a different valley, and chapter 6 shows the hikers end up standing on the same rock — the purely actual, simple, necessary source of everything.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes the whole book click is **dependence here and now**. Every causal proof asks not ‘what happened first?’ but ‘what is this thing relying on, at this very moment, simply to exist and act?’ Once someone sees that the cup relies on the desk, the desk on the floor, the water on its molecules, and that an endless chain of borrowers never produces a lender, the rest follows: there must be something that borrows nothing — no potency to be actualized, no parts to be held together, no existence to be received — and such a thing can only be one and has to be God.

The usual reason it fails to click is that listeners hear ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’ and ‘God’ as ‘a very big being’. They then reach for beginningless cosmologies or ‘who made God?’, both of which answer an argument no one made. Your first job, in almost every conversation, is to replace those two pictures: *first* means underived, and *God* means subsistent being itself, not the largest item in the inventory.

audiences.startingPoint: Trusts physics as our best picture of reality; suspects theology of gap-filling; often assumes the argument is about the Big Bang.
audiences.approach: Lead with the **Aristotelian** proof and everyday examples. Emphasize at once that the argument grants a beginningless universe and has nothing to predict or measure — it concerns what any physical theory presupposes. Distinguish explaining how something got here from what keeps it existing now (the water in the coffee). When quantum mechanics or inertia comes up, use the line-drawing and metal-detector images: physics’ silence about causation is an artifact of mathematical abstraction, not a discovery. Offer the **Neo-Platonic** ‘what holds it together right now?’ as a second route.
audiences.openingQuestion: When a physicist explains why this table holds up that cup, is she explaining what happened in the past, or what’s going on right now?
audiences.avoid: Don’t attack science, cite scientific ‘evidence for God’, or use fine-tuning; don’t let the conversation become about whether the universe had a beginning.

audiences.startingPoint: Already believes in objective, necessary, discovered truths; may happily accept abstract objects existing ‘nowhere’.
audiences.approach: Use the **Augustinian** proof. Start by agreeing: realism about numbers and propositions is right, and nominalism and conceptualism fail. Then press the question of *where* abstract objects can exist: if they are causally inert, how do we know them and how do they make things what they are? Show the animality problem for Forms and Welty’s relevance condition. Once they concede abstractions live only in minds, move to necessity (contingent minds can’t ground eternal truths), the interlocking system, and pure actuality.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would 2 + 2 = 4 have been true if no human had ever existed — and if so, what kind of reality does that truth have?
audiences.avoid: Don’t treat Platonism as silly; don’t skip the argument that a necessary intellect must be purely actual, or you’ll end with a ‘cosmic library’ rather than God.

audiences.who: Analytic philosophy student (Humean or Kantian training)
audiences.startingPoint: Knows Hume on causation, Kant on the cosmological argument, Frege on existence and possible-worlds modal reasoning; expects the arguments to be refuted in a textbook paragraph.
audiences.approach: Engage the premises precisely. Use the **Thomistic** and **rationalist** proofs. Answer the conceivability argument with trilateral/triangle and Anscombe’s point; answer Kenny with Klima and Knasas; answer Kant by distinguishing metaphysical necessity grounded in pure actuality from ‘existence by definition’; answer the big conjunctive fact by rejecting Platonic propositions and entailment-only explanation. Show that the textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is a straw man even Le Poidevin admits no one held.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which contemporary critic can you name who quotes an actual defender of the cosmological argument using the premise ‘everything has a cause’?
audiences.avoid: Don’t bluff about technical literature; don’t appeal to authority or to how many historical philosophers agreed — engage the argument on its merits.

audiences.who: Casual skeptic raised on New Atheist talking points
audiences.startingPoint: ‘Who made God?’, ‘science explains everything’, ‘one god further’, ‘faith is belief without evidence’.
audiences.approach: Spend the first minutes removing caricatures, calmly and with good humor: no ‘everything has a cause’, no Big Bang premise, no god of the gaps, no design argument. Then give one short proof — often the Aristotelian with the cup and desk — and show why ‘who made God?’ asks what actualized the potentials of that which has none. Use the triangularity analogy for ‘one god further’.
audiences.openingQuestion: If I could show you that the most famous objection to these arguments attacks something none of their defenders ever said, would you be willing to look at what they actually say?
audiences.avoid: Don’t be smug or quote Feser’s sharpest put-downs; don’t try to cover all five proofs or jump to religion-specific claims.

audiences.who: Believer with a ‘very powerful person in the sky’ picture of God
audiences.startingPoint: Believes in God but imagines him as a big being among beings, in time, with changing moods; may find arguments unnecessary or even irreverent.
audiences.approach: Use the **Neo-Platonic** proof and chapter 6 on simplicity, analogy and immutability. Show that a composite, changing god would need a cause and could have rivals — a superangel, not God. Explain that analogy lets us speak truly of God’s love and knowledge without shrinking him. Present natural theology as ‘faith grounded in reason’ (chapter 6 on miracles and faith), not as a rival to faith.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God were made of parts, what would hold those parts together?
audiences.avoid: Don’t make them feel their piety is naive; don’t present immutability as God being cold or unresponsive — stress that love is willing the good, not a passing emotion.

audiences.startingPoint: Senses a sacred ground of everything; resists a ‘separate’ God; may identify the divine with the universe or with consciousness.
audiences.approach: Affirm the insight that everything depends on a ground of being — that is the heart of the proofs. Then show why that ground cannot be the universe itself: the world changes, has parts and is contingent, while the ground must be simple, unchanging and necessary (chapter 6 against pantheism and panentheism). Stress conservation: God is more intimately present to everything than anything else, because he is keeping it in existence now.
audiences.openingQuestion: Can something that is always changing and made of parts be the ultimate reason anything exists at all?
audiences.avoid: Don’t caricature their view or rush to institutional religion; don’t describe God as distant — the doctrine of conservation makes him maximally present.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I know the argument: everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, and that’s God. But then what caused God? You can’t have it both ways.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed — that argument would be hopeless. But none of the five proofs in Feser’s book uses it. Take the first one. It never says everything has a cause. It says whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to actualize it. Your coffee can’t cool itself; the air does it. Do you think a mere potential could make itself actual?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No, but that’s a convenient redefinition. You pick a rule that lets God slip through. And anyway, maybe the universe had no beginning. Some cosmologists think the Big Bang came out of an earlier universe.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The rule isn’t new — it’s Aristotle’s analysis of change, two thousand years old and used for nothing theological at first. And Feser grants you the beginningless universe. The question isn’t what started things; it’s what’s keeping this cup of coffee in existence right now. Its water exists only because its matter is actually water rather than loose hydrogen and oxygen — which depends on the atoms, which depends on particles, all at this very moment. That’s a chain where each link borrows its power from the next, like a desk holding a cup only because the floor holds the desk.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Physics doesn’t talk about ‘actualizing potentials’. It has equations. And quantum mechanics has events with no cause at all — radioactive decay is random.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Physics describes the world mathematically and leaves out whatever can’t be quantified — the later Russell admitted it tells us structure, not what the structured stuff is. Absence of a cause from the equations is like absence of color from a line drawing: an artifact of the method. And a lead atom decaying at random still decays because of what it is, and still exists only because something keeps it existing. Indeterministic isn’t unintelligible.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, suppose the chain needs a bottom. Why not let the bottom be the universe itself, or the laws of physics? Why add God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because whatever ends the chain can’t be borrowing anything — no potential waiting to be actualized, no parts needing to be held together. The universe changes and has parts; so do the Big Bang and a multiverse. Laws are either descriptions of how things behave, which presuppose the things, or something the universe must somehow participate in, which needs explaining. And notice: if the universe really were necessary and uncaused, it would have divine attributes. You’d be a pantheist, not an atheist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Or there’s no bottom. Each state of things is explained by the one before, forever. Every member explained; no need for anything extra.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: For chains through time — your grandfather, your father, you — Feser actually agrees that could go back forever. But the chain I’m describing isn’t through time; it’s the stack holding you up right now. A mirror reflecting a mirror reflecting a mirror, infinitely, still needs a real face somewhere. An infinite pile of IOUs is never money. A brush handle a mile long, or infinitely long, still can’t move itself. Adding borrowers doesn’t produce a lender.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Honestly, this all sounds like a god of the gaps. We don’t know yet what underlies particles. Give science time.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A gap argument says, ‘we can’t explain this yet, so God.’ This says: whatever science finds underneath, it will be something that changes, has parts and could have been otherwise — because those are features of anything physical. The premise isn’t a gap in our knowledge; it’s what any possible scientific discovery would still presuppose. Let me try a different road: do you think everything has an explanation, even if we never find it?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Most things. But I’m happy to say the universe is just there. A brute fact. Explanation has to stop somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Stop there and every explanation built on it becomes an illusion. Suppose a book stays up because it rests on a shelf, and the shelf stays up for no reason at all — have you explained the book? The shelf has nothing to lend. And you’d never accept ‘it just happened, no reason’ in a lab. Why accept it only for the question of why anything exists? That’s the rationalist proof in a nutshell.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s where I actually am: I’m a mathematician. I’m sure 2 + 2 = 4 is true whether or not anyone thinks it. But that’s just Platonism. It doesn’t need God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then you’re already halfway down the Augustinian road — you reject nominalism and conceptualism, and so does Feser. The question is where such truths can live. If they float in a third realm, they can’t do anything — so how do they make triangles triangular, and how could we ever know them? And ‘animality itself’ would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual thing can be. Abstract things exist only in things or in minds. Truths that would hold if no humans existed need a mind that isn’t contingent — a necessary intellect.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So now you’ve got a cosmic mathematician, an unmoved mover, a necessary being. That’s three different things. Maybe a committee.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Chapter 6 takes that on directly. Anything with parts has potential, so what’s purely actual is simple; anything with potential has parts, so what’s simple is purely actual. A necessary mind can’t depend on being actualized, so it’s purely actual too. And two purely actual beings couldn’t differ — any difference would be a part or a potential. So it’s one reality described five ways, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both naming Venus.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then it’s the most complex thing imaginable — it knows everything, can do anything. Dawkins’ point: a designer would be more complex than what it designs, so it needs explaining even more.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Dawkins aims that at design arguments — eyes, flagella, probabilities. These proofs agree with him that anything complex needs a cause. That’s precisely why they conclude to something absolutely simple. The atheist’s alternatives — universe, laws, multiverse — are the complex ones.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But ‘simple’ and ‘omniscient and omnipotent and good’? Those are different properties. That’s incoherent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Different descriptions, same reality. ‘Power’ and ‘knowledge’ are distinct in us because we’re composite. Applied to God they’re used analogically — literally, but not in exactly our sense. It’s strange, but physics has taught us to expect strangeness at deep levels: something can behave like both a wave and a particle. The ultimate level of reality would stretch our concepts even further.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even if the metaphysics works, children die of cancer. An all-good, all-powerful being would stop that. Your God is contradicted by the world.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s the most serious question you’ve asked, and I won’t pretend it’s easy to feel. But logically, omnipotence doesn’t include doing contradictions, and some goods — mercy, courage, compassion, forgiveness — can’t exist without evils to face. Mackie, who pressed the logical version hardest, eventually conceded it fails. The probabilistic version says we can’t see a reason, so there probably isn’t one. But if there are sound independent proofs of a good, all-powerful God, then there is a reason, even when we can’t see it — the way a child can’t yet see why some hard things were good for him.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: It still feels like you believed first and built arguments to fit.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Maybe some believers do; and Thomas Nagel admitted he hoped there is no God and suspected that fear shapes a lot of secular thinking. Either way, motives don’t make premises true or false. So — which premise do you actually reject? That change is real? That a potential can’t actualize itself? That an infinite chain of borrowed power needs a lender?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not convinced. But I’ll admit I was attacking arguments nobody makes. Suppose I granted it all — does it prove Christianity?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: No, and Feser says so. Natural theology stops at one simple, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, good cause of everything. Whether that God has revealed himself is the next question — that’s where miracles and history come in, and where the real debate among theists begins. If you want, let’s take just one proof — the Thomistic one, about the difference between what a thing is and that it is — and go through it slowly next time.

socratic: Could a merely potential state of affairs — coldness that isn’t yet there — do anything at all, including make itself actual?
Is explaining how your coffee got into the cup the same as explaining what keeps it existing as coffee right now?
If a stick has no power of its own to move a stone, does making the stick longer — even infinitely long — give it any?
Can something be held together by one of its own parts, without our then asking what holds that part to the rest?
Would the Pythagorean theorem have been true a billion years ago, before any human mind existed? Where was it true?
If I describe a unicorn to you perfectly, have I thereby told you whether unicorns exist? What does that suggest about a thing’s existence?
Would you ever accept, in a laboratory, the explanation ‘there’s no reason — it just happened’? What would make the existence of things different?
If every block in a pile is red, is the pile red? If every thing in a collection could fail to exist, could the collection?
How could we tell two beings apart if neither had any parts, any potential or anything the other lacked?
If God were made of parts, what would put those parts together?
If ‘God’ meant a being alongside other beings, would anything be left to explain why there are beings at all?
When physics gives a mathematical description of a system, does it tell us everything about the system — or only what can be described mathematically?

traps.trap: Opening with the Big Bang or ‘the universe must have had a beginning’.
traps.fix: Say up front that every causal proof grants a beginningless universe; the issue is dependence here and now. Use the cup-desk-floor or water-molecule example.

traps.trap: Saying ‘everything has a cause’ as shorthand.
traps.fix: Always state the precise principle: whatever goes from potential to actual, whatever is composite, whatever has its existence from another, or whatever is contingent needs a cause; everything has an explanation.

traps.trap: Presenting the proofs as the ‘best explanation’ or most probable hypothesis.
traps.fix: Frame them as demonstrations whose premises any scientific theory presupposes; invite the listener to identify a false premise or invalid step rather than to weigh probabilities.

traps.trap: Describing God as a very big, very powerful being — a cosmic engineer or superperson.
traps.fix: Describe God as subsistent being itself, purely actual and simple — not a being among beings — which is exactly why ‘who made God?’ and ‘one god further’ misfire.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there is a first cause’ and conceding it might not be God.
traps.fix: Always include Stage 2: from pure actuality (or simplicity, or necessity) derive uniqueness, immutability, eternity, immateriality, goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience.

traps.trap: Firing all five proofs at once, or piling on jargon.
traps.fix: Choose one proof suited to the listener, anchor every term in an everyday example, and mention the convergence only after one proof has landed.

traps.trap: Jumping from natural theology to specific doctrines (Trinity, scripture, Resurrection) as if the proofs established them.
traps.fix: Be explicit that the proofs establish classical theism only; revealed claims need further argument, with miracles as the bridge.

traps.trap: Adopting Feser’s combative tone — calling objections ‘incompetent’ or critics ignorant.
traps.fix: Keep his content, drop the heat: show that an objection targets a caricature, then ask what the person thinks of the actual premise. Confidence belongs in the argument, not the adjectives.

connections.note: The introduction sets out the book’s method (informal two-stage statement, formal statement, objections), the five proofs’ sources, and the claim that the real debate is among theists; the capstone’s summary of the project and the two-stage structure builds directly on it.

Supplies the toolkit — act and potency, the principle of causality, hierarchical series, the PPC, the meaning of ‘first’ — and the template Stage 2 derivation of the attributes that every later proof reuses; the ‘pure actuality’ node of the convergence argument.

The ‘simplicity’ node of the convergence argument; also introduces the sense/reference distinction and analogical predication that make the identity of the five conclusions and the unity of the attributes intelligible.
The only non-causal proof and the ‘divine intellect’ node; it explains how the first cause has intellect and why abstract objects cannot serve as non-divine necessary beings.

The ‘subsistent existence itself’ node; its essence/existence distinction is, for Feser, the deepest explanation of why creatures depend on God at every moment, and it answers Hume’s ‘why a first cause?’ and the composition charge.
The ‘necessary being’ node; it grounds the demand for explanation (PSR) that underlies all the causal principles and notes how the five proofs complement one another.

Chapter 6’s background principles (PPC, agere sequitur esse, analogy of being) and the Unity section, which proves the five proofs reach one and the same God — the backbone of Stage B of the capstone argument — plus simplicity, immutability, eternity and necessity.

The remaining attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility) and God’s relation to the world — conservation, concurrence, the rejection of pantheism, occasionalism and deism, and miracles as the bridge to revealed religion.

The first half of the objection chapter — the ‘What caused God?’ straw man and its history, the universe as necessary being, no-cause and no-beginning objections, composition, the attributes gap, and the ontological and god-of-the-gaps charges — feeds items 1–10 and 17 of the objection handbook.

The second half — scientism, brute-fact laws, the ‘more complex designer’, ‘one god further’, the God of the philosophers, evil, hiddenness, rationalization, and what counts as a demonstration — feeds items 18–20 and the capstone’s section on demonstration and controversy.
